ru: Ря́дом с ле́сом стоя́т ста́рые да́чи.
en_alt: Old dachas stand next to the forest.
note: «ря́дом с» is equally 'next to'; the alternative stops the word-bank drill rejecting it.

ru: В выходны́е мы е́дем на да́чу.

en_alt: Heat was coming from the little door of the stove.
note: Imperfective «шёл» also reads as a past continuous in English.

ru: У шка́фчика бы́ли две ма́леньких две́рцы.

en_alt: Someone is knocking on the door.
note: 'at' and 'on the door' are both idiomatic for «стучи́т в дверь».

ru: Из-за дво́йки его́ не пусти́ли гуля́ть.
en_alt: Because of the failing grade they did not let him go out.
note: The Russian is an impersonal plural «не пусти́ли»; the literal reading is worth accepting too.

en_alt: A big garden grows in front of the palace.
note: «большо́й» is glossed 'big'; both renderings are correct.

en_alt: The tourists are looking round the beautiful palace.
note: «осма́тривать» is literally 'look round / view'; the alt is closer to the Russian.

en_alt: The knight rescued the maiden from the dragon.
note: 'rescued' is an equally standard rendering of «спас» here.

ru: На уро́ке та́нцев де́вочкам разда́ли я́ркие ле́нты.
en_alt: In the dance lesson the girls were handed bright ribbons.
note: «уро́к» is 'lesson'; the alt tracks the Russian more closely.

ru: Ле́том я гощу́ у де́да в дере́вне.

en_alt: In the photo are my grandfathers.
note: The Russian fronts the locative phrase; the inverted English is equally valid.

ru: Мы бы́ли в гостя́х у де́душки.
note: «быть в гостя́х у» is idiomatic and 'were visiting' is its standard English.

en_alt: Grandfather loves telling stories.
note: Gerund and infinitive are both natural after 'loves'.

ru: Мы регуля́рно звони́м де́душкам по выходны́м.
en_alt: We regularly call our grandfathers at weekends.
note: «по выходны́м» is habitual plural, which 'at weekends' renders more exactly.

en_alt: We observed the soldiers' actions.
note: «наблюда́ть за» is literally 'observe'.

en: The medicine began to take effect.
en_alt: The medicine began its action.
note: 'began its action' is translationese; 'take effect' is what an English speaker writes for «начало́ де́йствие».

ru: Де́ло в том, что я опозда́ла.
en_alt: The thing is, I was late.
note: Comma-spliced version is the commoner English form of the same idiom.

en_alt: Hi! How are things?
note: 'How are things?' is closer to «Как дела́?» while staying idiomatic.

ru: Он рассказа́л мне о своём де́ле.
en_alt: He told me about his business.
note: 'case' is a sense the headword gloss 'matter' does not cover; 'business/affair' is the commoner reading of «своём де́ле».

en: He has many things to do today.
en_alt: He has a lot to do today.
note: 'matters to deal with' pads the Russian; «мно́го дел» is simply 'many things to do'.

ru: У меня́ к тебе́ ва́жное де́ло.
en_alt: I have an important matter to discuss with you.
note: «к тебе́» implies bringing the matter to the person; the alt makes that explicit.

en_alt: On these days I will be at home.
note: Bare 'These days' can be misread as 'nowadays', which the Russian does not mean.

ru: В таки́х больши́х деньга́х легко́ запу́таться.
en_alt: It is easy to get confused with such large sums of money.
note: «запу́таться» is equally 'get confused'.

ru: В студе́нческие го́ды прихо́дится знать счёт деньга́м.
note: «знать счёт деньга́м» is an idiom and 'keep count of your money' carries it.

ru: В о́тпуске он распоряжа́лся деньга́ми о́чень легкомы́сленно.
en_alt: On holiday he handled his money very frivolously.
note: «легкомы́сленно» is 'frivolously/thoughtlessly' rather than 'carelessly'.

ru: Я заплати́л за биле́т свои́ми деньга́ми.

en_alt: I have no money.
note: Both negations are standard English for «нет де́нег».

ru: Он потра́тил все де́ньги на кни́ги.
en_alt: He spent all the money on books.
note: The Russian has no possessive, so 'all the money' is the more literal option.

ru: Врач е́здит по далёким деревня́м ка́ждую неде́лю.
en_alt: The doctor travels round the distant villages every week.
note: «далёким» is glossed 'distant' and «е́здит» need not be 'drives'.

ru: В э́том краю́ мно́го ма́леньких дереве́нь.
В далёких деревня́х ещё то́пят пе́чи дрова́ми.
en_alt: In distant villages they still heat the stoves with firewood.
note: The Russian is an active impersonal plural, which the alt preserves.

ru: Из дере́вни в го́род веду́т у́зкие доро́ги.

en_alt: The yard has become overgrown with old trees.
note: The pluperfect has no anchoring context here; the present perfect is at least as good.

en_alt: A severe frost harms the young trees.
note: «си́льный» is 'strong/severe'; both English adjectives are natural with 'frost'.

en_alt: We were walking among the trees.
note: Imperfective «гуля́ли» supports a past continuous too.

ru: Он рассказа́л исто́рию во всех дета́лях.
en_alt: He told the story in all its details.
note: «во всех дета́лях» is plural; the alt keeps that.

ru: Меха́ник заказа́л но́вую дета́ль для маши́ны.
note: 'part' is the right English here, but the headword gloss 'detail' does not cover the machine-part sense — the gloss is probably what needs widening.

en_alt: She loves old detective stories.
note: «лю́бит» is glossed 'to love'; both readings are correct.

ru: Ба́бушка пе́ред сном расска́зывает де́тям ста́рые ска́зки.
en_alt: Before bed grandmother tells the children old fairy tales.
note: «ба́бушка» is glossed 'grandmother'; both are natural.

ru: На собра́нии до́лго говори́ли о де́тях.

en_alt: We bought the children presents.
note: The double-object order matches the Russian dative directly.

en_alt: The children are playing in the courtyard.
note: «двор» is glossed 'courtyard'; both renderings are correct.

ru: Ве́чером мать забира́ет дете́й из са́дика.
Воспита́тельница вы́шла на прогу́лку с детьми́.

en_alt: The parents came out of the nursery.
note: «вы́йти из» is literally 'come/go out of'.

ru: Мы покра́сили де́тскую в жёлтый цвет.

en_alt: He told us about his childhood.
note: The Russian has no addressee; 'us' is invented, so the audience-free 'talked about' is the accurate rendering.

ru: Своё де́тство он провёл в дере́вне.

en: He is a well-known cultural figure.
en_alt: He is a well-known figure in culture.
note: 'a figure in culture' is not idiomatic English; «де́ятель ку́льтуры» is 'a cultural figure'.

en_alt: They put up a monument to the great figure.
note: The Russian is active impersonal plural with «поста́вили» = 'put up'.

en_alt: The company is engaged in charitable activity.
note: Both renderings of «занима́ется» are standard.

ru: Без де́ятельности он не мог жить.

en_alt: There was no gin left in the bar.
note: «не оста́лось» is past tense, so the past English is at least as accurate.

en_alt: People rarely drink gin without tonic.
note: The Russian is an active impersonal plural, which the alt preserves.

en_alt: He ordered gin with tonic.
note: 'a gin and tonic' is the idiomatic drink name; the alt gives the literal «с то́ником».

en_alt: These jeans are comfortable to walk in.
note: Equally valid English rendering of the impersonal «удо́бно ходи́ть».

en_alt: The doctor recommended a diet for him.
note: «посове́товал» is 'advised/recommended'; the en_gb adds 'to go on', which the alt avoids.

en_alt: Big speakers stood on the stage.
note: «больши́е» is glossed 'big'; both are natural.
«включи́ть ... гро́мче» is colloquial but idiomatic and the English matches it.

ru: На конфере́нции дире́кторам заво́дов вручи́ли награ́ды.

en_alt: The teachers talked to the director.
note: 'spoke with' and 'talked to' are both standard for «говори́ли с».

en_alt: I bought a new hard disk.
note: «жёсткий диск» is 'hard disk' as well as 'hard drive', and keeps the headword visible.

en: This disc can no longer be read.
en_alt: This disc is no longer readable.
note: 'the disc no longer reads' is not English; the Russian reflexive is passive.

en_alt: The table is two metres long.
note: The commoner English phrasing of «длино́й два ме́тра».

en: Stones lie on the bottom of the river.
en_alt: There are stones at the bottom of the river.
note: 'the river bottom' is clunky and the existential drops «лежа́т», which English can render literally as 'lie'.

en_alt: The boat went down to the bottom.
note: «опусти́лась» is 'went/sank down'; both are accurate.
Fixed formula; 'Welcome to Moscow!' is its only English.

en_alt: Good always conquers evil.
note: «побежда́ет» is equally 'conquers/triumphs over'.
«идёт дождь» is idiomatic and 'It is raining outside' is its standard English.

en_alt: We were walking in the rain.
note: Imperfective «шли» supports a past continuous too.

ru: Мы спря́тались от дождя́ под де́ревом.
en_alt: We hid from the rain under a tree.
note: «спря́таться» is literally 'to hide'.

en_alt: The police have no evidence.
note: In a police context «доказа́тельства» is normally 'evidence' in English.

ru: Я записа́лся к до́ктору на за́втра.

en_alt: Doctor, I have a headache.
note: Both are standard English for «у меня́ боли́т голова́».
'left ... at home' is the idiomatic English for «забы́л до́ма».

en_alt: Without documents you will not be let in.
note: The Russian impersonal plural has no explicit 'they'; the passive alt avoids inventing one.

ru: Он рабо́тает с докуме́нтами весь день.
